text:
Gray and damp to start this Sunday, with a few lingering showers that should wrap up by mid to late morning. After that we get a dry afternoon, still mostly cloudy but mild enough, with a high near 51. A light jacket does the job.

Showers return tonight, on and off from around 8, adding up to about a tenth of an inch, with a low near 42. Monday looks like the wetter of the two days. The best chance is the morning commute, roughly 4 to 10, peaking around 7, then it turns more scattered through the afternoon. The high is near 51 again. The models don't agree on how much rain we get, with one fairly dry and two much wetter, so I'd lean wet and keep the umbrella by the door.

Tuesday and Veterans Day look a bit drier, with only a stray shower. The thing to watch is a coastal storm late in the week, which could bring a rain and snow mix Thursday into Friday, possibly the first real snow of the season. One outlook keeps us drier but colder, so the details are still up in the air.

AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: Precipitation will continue to slowly wind down through the early morning hours as an upper level low pinwheels away to the east. While most of the precipitation is falling as rain or drizzle, temperatures in the higher elevations and portions of the Northeast Kingdom are in the low to mid 30s; our sensor on Mt Mansfield at just short of 4000 ft is reading 28F as of 1 am. Therefore expect these areas are seeing periods of snow, though ground temperatures should be warm enough to preclude any accumulation below 2500 ft. Cameras on some of the higher elevation roads in the Northeast Kingdom courtesy of VTrans do appear to show a bit of snow falling with no accumulation noted, though it's difficult to discern for sure due to darkness and thick fog. These lingering showers will taper to an end by mid to late morning or so, allowing for a dry Sunday afternoon. Highs will be in the low 40s to low 50s, with a bit of a brisk wind at 5 to 15 mph with local gusts to around 20 mph. Additional rounds of showers are expected then through the first half of this week as we remain under the influence of a large upper level low gyrating over eastern Canada. Multiple shortwaves rotating around the base of this low will pivot overhead, keeping the weather unsettled over the next few days. Much like our current system, much of the shower activity will fall as rain, especially during the daylight hours, but some snow will be possible across the higher terrain and portions of the Adirondacks/Northeast Kingdom, especially overnight. Any accumulation will be minimal below 2500 ft, but we'll be watching closely to see if Mt Mansfield is able to break the record for latest 1" of snowfall (Nov 9). Highs will be in the low/mid 40s to low 50s each day, with lows falling into the upper 20s to mid/upper 30s. Winds will remain on the breezy side, but not strong enough to cause any significant impacts. KEY MESSAGE 2: The large Hudson Bay low will continue to dominate the weather across our area, bringing multiple shortwaves into region through the weekend. Wednesday should see lingering, terrain driven mix of rain and snow showers throughout the day. Models on Thursday remain torn on the timing and placement of warm front ahead of the developing low in the Ohio Valley. The solutions could bring a rain- snow mix, or keep things further south and keep our area relatively dry during the day. For Friday and the weekend, models are still keying in on significant closed low swinging down through the Mid- Atlantic region and then up the coastline, bringing several shots of rain and rain/snow mix over the weekend. The current runs are leaning towards a wetter solution for our region which could bring the first significant snow of the season. The details should come into better focus over the next few days.

WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Showers were stubborn to move into northern areas today and remained mainly in southern parts of the region. That said, scattered showers are expected tonight, including northern sections. These showers will end as a brief period of snow Sunday morning for Coos County, New Hampshire. A trace to 3 inches accumulation is possible, though mainly in the White Mountains. The rest of Sunday will become partly sunny with highs in the mid-40s to low 50s. The next system will quickly move in Sunday night with more showers. Showers are likely on Monday, especially for the morning. They will become more widely scattered as the afternoon progresses. Highs will be in the 40s with lows in the 30s. Tuesday and Veterans Day looks a little drier now, though a few showers can’t be ruled out both days. Our eyes then turn to a potential coastal storm late in the week, though it can still change as the time is pretty far out. At this time, Thursday is expected to have increasing clouds with a rain/snow mix by afternoon, continuing overnight and through Friday. Some snow accumulation isn’t out of the question, even in the valleys, but there’s still plenty of time for things to change. Showers and mountain snow showers may continue into Saturday with highs mainly in the 30s and lows in the 20s. It’s something we’ll keep an eye on during the week.

Mountain snowflakes, and a light accumulation, are possible for northern summits (especially in New Hampshire). Sunday looks drier, with morning clouds giving way to a window of afternoon sun — which may illuminate a light dusting of summit snow. Highs will be near 50. Early next week looks seasonably cool, with several chances for rain showers and minor mountain snow accumulations between Monday and Veterans Day. Highs reach the 40s to around 50. Drier weather looks to return by Thursday and Friday. However, expect lots of clouds and chillier temperatures. Highs will be near 40.
